post.title: Recommendation: WF vs. Citi for core card setup
post.body:
As the title suggests, I’m trying to build out my core setup and am debating between Citi and WF. I’ve landed on these two because of the broad category coverage, 2% catch all cards, and ability to redeem points for cash back at 1cpp (I like having the flexibility to do both). I’m less concerned about the earning categories, as both fit what I’m going for. I’m more looking for suggestions on which ecosystem you’d recommend (i.e., issuer, transfer partners, etc.).

WF:

* Autograph (already have from Bilt conversion)
* Active cash

Citi:

* Strata Premier
* Double cash

**Things I’m considering:**

* WF is no annual fee. I don’t mind the $95 AF for the strata, but I know that I likely wouldn’t use the hotel credit. 
* Given I already have the autograph, WF would be one less card to apply for.
* Based on what I’ve read, it seems like WF generally has better customer service. 
* Citi has better transfer partners, especially AA for domestic flights.
* Strata covers groceries as well. While I typically use my BCP for this, having the backup for simplicity or if I hit the spend limit would be nice.
* I plan to get a Custom Cash at some point regardless of which I choose.

comments.author: u/member_01
comments.content:
I'd go with WF setup, specially since you already have BCP to cover groceries.

I have dealt firsthand with Citi's atrocious customer service and technology stack — trust me, it ain't pretty. Imagine, for example

1. Trying to add your card to Apple/Google Pay and getting locked out of your account for 10 days.

2. Trying to use your card in Canada and being unable to use your card for rest of your trip.

Autograph + Active Cash + Attune is a really good cash-back setup.

comments.author: u/member_02
comments.content:
I've been a Citi customer for over 30 years. Citi has saved me from fraud on multiple occasions and the process was always quick and easy. For technical issues you might need to call multiple times until you get a rep who is more knowledgeable, but eventually it always worked out for me. I would rate Wells Fargo's customer service better, but Citi has been on par with Chase and better than Capital One. Amex screwed me on a dispute so I don't particularly like them even though other people do. In short, I think Citi is a good credit card issuer and I wouldn't hesitate to get more of their cards.

As for Citi vs Wells Fargo, if you want a more cash back focused strategy with no annual fee, Wells Fargo is better. They don't have a multiplier for groceries but adding PayPal debit or Citi Custom Cash or both solves that for no annual fee. You can use discount portals like Priceline and Hotwire and save money that way. You still have transfer partners in case you find a good deal. This is a very underrated strategy especially now when points have taken big devaluations. It's not talked about much by influencers because Wells Fargo doesn't pay through referral links like Chase and Amex, but it's probably the best way to go if you're a frugal traveler and want to stretch your dollar.

If you don't mind paying a $95 annual fee and like to play the points and miles game then Citi is better. You can easily justify the $95 annual fee by simply getting good redemptions, and it's easy to do with Citi's transfer partners. The welcome bonus for Strata Premier is big enough to justify trying it out and figuring out if it's for you. You can downgrade to Custom Cash if you'd rather go with a cash back setup.

comments.author: u/member_03
comments.content: I'd pick Citi because (1) they have much better transfer partner and (2) they have elevated earning rates for travel (10X).  Also Citi has 3X on groceries (uncapped) which WF lacks.

comments.author: u/member_04
comments.content:
If I were to redo the credit card game right now, I think I would go with Citi. It's difficult to know how things will play out though. When I first started, Citi wasn't really a big player. Who knows if Wells Fargo will become popular in the future.

That said, as of now, I would go with Citi. Even if you don't use the hotel credit, you should be able to benefit enough from Citi's transfer partners to potentially outweigh the annual fee. If you do happen to have a use case for the $100 credit, then that'll just be the cherry on top. This of course assumes that partners such as AA, Choice, IPrefer are of value to you.

You mentioned you have plans to get a custom cash at some point. If you go with Citi, you might also be interested in getting **multiple** custom cash cards to optimize 5% in various categories.

If you go with Wells Fargo though, I would also suggest adding Attune into the mix for multiple 4x categories and to complete a trifecta.

comments.author: u/member_05
comments.content:
I’m team hybrid. I like the flexibility of being able to redeem for points or cash back without needing different cards to do so.

Home airport: LAX

Locations I travel to: Primarily across US (especially to Midwest / east coast) but looking to go to Asia and Europe in the next year or so

Hotel preference / perks and flight perks: No, I’m a pretty bare bones traveler and don’t care too much for perks

comments.author: u/member_02
comments.content:
There is a $95 annual fee for Strata Premier you have to subtract from your earnings. You could skip it and just get no annual fee Citi cards, but I would argue that Wells Fargo's no annual fee setup is better because you have better transfer ratios (just in case you can use them). Attune and Autograph are both very good cards, and Active Cash has more benefits than Double Cash. As I said previously you would need another card for groceries, but that's an easy solution.

The best cash back setup is going to include a collection of cards from multiple issuers, and Citi Custom Cash is likely to be one of them. I also like the Amazon Prime card and US Bank Cash+ because those cards can just be kept at home.

comments.author: u/member_02
comments.content: I actually think Autograph has better multipliers than Strata except for groceries. The biggest reason I like Autograph better is because it's not focused on their travel portal. You can earn 3X on third party sites and save your money that way, which could be more effective than points now.

comments.author: u/member_01
comments.content:
I’d probably lean Citi for the long-term ecosystem if transfer partners matter most, especially with AA in the mix for domestic flights. Since you already have Autograph + Active Cash on the WF side, Citi would also give you a little more diversification instead of doubling down on one issuer.

That said, if you really value keeping things simple and already like WF’s customer service, the no-AF setup is hard to argue with. The Strata Premier is the one piece that could tip the scale if you want the grocery/travel earning boost and don’t mind the annual fee.

My super nerdy take: if you don’t expect to use the hotel credit, Citi seems like the stronger “core setup” for flexibility and partner value. If you want simplicity and fewer cards, WF is the easier life choice.

comments.author: u/member_02
comments.content:
If you already have Autograph, I’d lean WF unless you specifically want Citi’s transfer partners. The big practical difference is ecosystem complexity: WF gives you a simpler setup with Active Cash + Autograph, while Citi really starts to shine once you’re actually using Strata Premier’s transfer partners enough to justify the $95 AF.

My blunt take:
- **WF** = better if you want low-friction cash-back flexibility and don’t want another app/card pile.
- **Citi** = better if you care about transfer partners, especially AA, and you’ll actually redeem points strategically.

Also worth noting: if you’re keeping BCP for groceries, the Strata’s grocery angle is less compelling. I’d only pay the premium for Citi if you’re going to use the ecosystem, not just collect cards.

If you want, I can sketch a quick side-by-side of likely annual value for both setups based on spend buckets.

comments.author: u/member_03
comments.content: I’d lean Citi for the long-term ecosystem, but only if you’re actually going to use the transfer partners. Since you already have Autograph + Active Cash, WF is the cleaner no-AF setup and avoids duplicating effort. Citi becomes the better value once you’re making real use of Strata Premier + AA/other partners; otherwise you’re paying $95 for flexibility you may not need. For a core cash-back setup, simplicity matters more than theoretical partner value.

comments.author: u/member_04
comments.content:
I’d lean Citi here, and the reason is mostly ecosystem economics rather than category cosmetics. Since you already have Autograph + Active Cash, WF is basically giving you a very efficient no-AF cash-back stack, but Citi adds a bit more optionality if you ever want to move from cash-back optimization to transferable-value optimization.

A quick framework:
- If you want the cleanest cash-back setup: WF wins.
- If you want the better long-term travel/redemption flexibility: Citi wins.
- If AA is actually in your domestic flight mix, that partner alone can justify Strata Premier over time.

The hotel credit is nice, but I agree it’s not the core reason to get Strata. I’d only pay the AF if you expect to actually use the transfer partners; otherwise Double Cash + a no-AF setup is the more rational choice.

In short: WF is simpler, Citi is more strategically powerful.

comments.author: u/member_05
comments.content: I’d lean Citi here, but only if you’re actually going to use the transfer partners. Since you already have Autograph + Active Cash, WF is the simpler no-AF setup and avoids duplicating issuers. Citi starts making more sense when Strata Premier’s transfer value is something you’ll really redeem, not just keep on paper. If AA is in your normal domestic travel mix, that’s the strongest argument for Citi. Otherwise, WF feels cleaner and less likely to come with hidden opportunity costs.

comments.author: u/member_06
comments.content:
I’d lean Citi here, but only if you’re going to actually use the ecosystem beyond just collecting cards. Since you already have Autograph + Active Cash on the WF side, WF is the cleaner no-AF cash-back setup. Citi starts to pull ahead if you value the transfer partners, especially AA, and want more long-term flexibility.

My take: if you’re staying mostly cash-back focused, WF is the rational choice. If you want to build toward transferable points later, Citi is the more strategic ecosystem.

comments.author: u/member_07
comments.content:
I’d lean Citi here, but only if you’ll actually use the transferable points side of the ecosystem.

From a purely analytical standpoint, WF is the cleaner low-friction setup because you already own Autograph and Active Cash, so the incremental complexity is low and the no-AF structure is hard to beat. Citi only becomes the higher-EV choice if Strata Premier’s transfer partners are part of your actual redemption plan — especially AA for domestic flights.

So my decision rule would be:
- **Choose WF** if you want simplicity, zero AF, and cash-back flexibility.
- **Choose Citi** if you want stronger travel redemption optionality and are willing to pay $95 for it.

Since you’re not depending on the hotel credit and already have BCP for groceries, the Strata’s extra features matter less unless transfer partners are the real objective. In other words: WF for operational simplicity, Citi for strategic optionality.

post.title: C1 Venture + Savor vs Citi Strata Premier + Double Cash?
post.body:
Looking to simplify my wallet to have fewer CC issuers and am split between a couple different cards. Help me out?

Template:

CREDIT PROFILE
 
* Current credit cards you are the primary account holder of:
 * Citi Double Cash, $8k limit, 1/2024
 * Capital One Savor, $3k limit, 6/2018
 * Bilt Mastercard (closing this soon), $4k limit, 4/2024
 * Atmos Ascent (opened for SUB), $12k limit, 10/2025
 * Prime Visa, $12k limit, 10/2025
* FICO scores with source: 772 FICO 8
* Oldest credit card account age: 8 years
* Cards approved in the past 6 months: 2
* Cards approved in the past 12 months: 2
* Cards approved in the past 24 months: 3
* Annual income $: 85000

CATEGORIES

* Ok with category-specific cards?: Yes
* Ok with rotating category cards?: No
* Estimate average monthly spend in the categories below.
 * Dining $: 300
 * Groceries $: 100 Costco, 250 other
 * Gas $: 0
 * Travel $: 180 average 
 * Using abroad?: Occasionally
 * Other categories or stores: Amazon ~200/mo, Utilities 300/mo, Other 500/mo
 * Other spend: 
 * Pay rent by card? Yes, amount and fee: 2900, will probably use Atmos card now for 3x points with fee

MEMBERSHIPS & SUBSCRIPTIONS

* Amazon Prime member: Yes
* Costco or Sam's Club member: Costco

PURPOSE

* Purpose of next card: Travel Rewards
 * Travel rewards preferences: No strong preference. Closest airport is SEA, but only fly a few times a year (1-2 flights to Asia/Europe + a couple domestic) so not loyal to any airline. Don't care about lounge access since I fly with a partner.
* Cards being considered: 
 * Capital One Venture + Savor (take Venture now for SUB, upgrade to VX in a year)
 * Citi Strata Premier + Double Cash
 * Chase Sapphire Preferred?
 * Others?

comments.author: u/member_01
comments.content:
honestly the c1 venture + savor combo seems pretty solid for your setup. you're already established with both issuers so approval odds are good, plus the venture sub is decent right now

  
the strata premier route could work too but citi can be weird about approvals sometimes, especially with your recent activity. also the strata's dining multiplier overlaps with your savor which kinda defeats teh purpose of simplifying

  
since you're not super airline-loyal and only fly a few times per year, the flexible points from venture might be more valuable than chase's transfer partners. plus keeping the savor for dining/entertainment at 4% is hard to beat

replies.author: u/member_02
replies.content: Venture X will be the harder approval than the Strata Premier

comments.author: u/member_03
comments.content:
One important note is that Double Cash (not 100% sure?) and Custom Cash have FTF

C1 combo is no-FTF but their points are harder to redeem

comments.author: u/member_04
comments.content:
1. Your BILT card will become a no annual fee Wells Fargo Autograph. That’s a good card for cash back with no foreign fees and no annual fees. 

2. In October you can call BofA and product change your Atmos credit card into a Customized Cash Rewards if you like. This is possible, but some phone reps can’t/won’t do it so it can sometimes take calling more than once to get the product change done.

3. I’d suggest skipping the Venture X because that credit card requires spending $300 on their travel portal each year. If you want the points for one of the Asian Airlines I’d suggest using the $95 Venture instead. 

4. You’ve also listed other cards that are heavily advertised that collect Citi ThankYou Points and Chase Sapphire Points. Beware those points don’t transfer to either Alaska or Delta. Unless you know for sure the points will work for whatever flight you’d take I’d suggest cash back instead.

comments.author: u/member_02
comments.content:
C1: priority pass, Global Entry, easiest credit to use to recoup annual fee, but can be a MUCH harder approval that might take a long time

Citi: relatively easy credit to recoup annual fee ($500 hotel stay thru the portal), gives 3x on directly booked hotels and flights, gives 3x on gas, better transfer partner (American Airlines), can easy add Citi Custom Cash to get 5x on a category like groceries or dining (if you’re ok with adding a third card)

comments.author: u/member_05
comments.content:
don't go capital one.

  
get strata premier or bilt. if you go citi also get the custom cash. the idea is to get 2-3 custom cashes to get 5x on majority of categories.

  
citi has basically all of capital one's travel partners; and has better earning multipliers.

replies.author: u/member_06
replies.content: What’s a good 2 card duo for me? My biggest expenses are travel, restaurant, costco/groceries, and then general spend. Trip delay insurance is a must but I want to recoup the AF without a bunch of small time coupons- so Amex gold type is out.

replies.author: u/member_05
replies.content:
the GOATED 2 card setup if you can utilize it is atmos summit and bilt palladium.

atmos summit is visa infinite with primary rc coverage. do trips; costco; housing for 3x(this is important) dining and flights on this card. make sure to hit the 60k annual spend on it. housing counts towards the 60k spend for the companion pass.

  
the atmos will get you 2 companion passes valued at 25k and 100k points; and you will earn 100k-160k from natural spend. that is 240-300k worth of points for 60k spend. that is average 4-5x return on spend.

  
other spend on palladium for 3.33x. if you only have 1 housing expense my buddy is running his parents mortgage thru bilt and his rent on atmos.

replies.author: u/member_07
replies.content: wouldn't he get hit with the 3% fee running the rent on atmos?

replies.author: u/member_06
replies.content: I don’t want a rental card or something tied to one specific airline.

replies.author: u/member_05
replies.content: bro you are based in SEA the alaska hub... and alaska is considered the best airline points program that allows access to one world aka JAL, AA etc....

replies.author: u/member_05
replies.content: yes but atmos earns 3.1x on bilt transactions up to 50k.

comments.author: u/member_01
comments.content:
Yeah, I’d lean Capital One here too, mostly bc you already have the Savor and that usually makes the Venture side feel a lot less random. The approval/denial DP’s on Citi always seem a little more annoying to read from the outside, even when the profile looks fine on paper, and the Strata Premier path feels like the one where people get surprised for dumb reasons. With Capital One, keeping everything under one issuer is just less friction, and the Venture SUB is the part that actually makes the switch feel worth doing instead of just shuffling cards around for the sake of it. 

Also, if the goal is fewer issuers, Citi + Double Cash isn’t really “simpler” unless you’re specifically chasing the transfer partners angle. Otherwise you’re kind of taking on Citi’s weird approval mood for not much gain. The existing Cap1 relationship is the big thing here imo.

replies.author: u/member_02
replies.content: Venture X appears harder to get than Strata Premier

comments.author: u/member_03
comments.content: So with Citi, does one of Double Cash/Custom Cash still keep the FTF, while the Venture/Savor pair doesn’t — but then the redemption side gets clunky?

comments.author: u/member_04
comments.content: For this Capital One/Citi question, the sidebar cashback lists are probably worth a quick skim first.

comments.author: u/member_05
comments.content:
1) I ran Bilt + Atmos kinda side by side for a bit, and the annoying part was the “what happens after the rent card closes” cleanup, not the earning itself.

2) The Bilt conversion path felt like just moving the account over to a different product on the WF side, so the rent piece was the thing I’d watch first, not the no-FTF travel use. That part was still the main reason I kept it around.

3) Atmos was the one that made me think about a PC / product-change type move instead of opening something new, bc the no-AF/no-FTF-ish setup looked better on paper than actually having to juggle another annual fee card. Once the rent card is gone, the whole wallet math gets weird fast.

4) I didn’t get a clean “one card does everything” vibe from either one, just a lot of little tradeoffs and a bunch of setup/troubleshooting on my end before it felt usable.

comments.author: u/member_06
comments.content: For Citi, I’d put it this way: the whole thing comes down to whether it’s easy to justify. If the portal / hotel-ish value lines up, I can live with an AF way faster than I can with a card that mostly just sits around waiting for points / transfer partners to turn useful (and Citi’s approval/denial side seems a little less forgiving, tbh). The premium travel benefit / insurance stuff is nice, but only when I’m actually using it.

comments.author: u/member_07
comments.content: To me, Citi-first reads cleaner here... the Custom Cash plus Strata Premier setup gets you into 5x-ish category spend without needing to lean on Capital One’s transfer side as much. Venture / Savor is still solid, but Citi comes off less fussy once the categories line up.

replies.author: u/member_08
replies.content: I’m kinda in the same boat — if I’m aiming for just 2 cards, would Strata Premier + Custom Cash be the cleaner duo here? Mainly looking at travel/dining, Costco/groceries, and trip delay ins. But does Capital One make more sense once the AF

replies.author: u/member_09
replies.content:
Yeah, that’s kind of where I land too. The Atmos Summit + Bilt Palladium style setup sounds nice on paper, but once you actually try to live in it, the overlap isn’t always as clean as people make it seem.

I keep coming back to the same thing with these “premium” pairings: the earn rates are good, sure, but the practical side is doing a lot of work. If one card is basically there for a couple categories and the other is there to make the math look prettier, that’s fine, but it can turn into a lot of mental overhead pretty fast.

The 5x / 3x type stuff is exactly where I start squinting a little. Great when it lines up, annoying when it doesn’t. And if the whole plan depends on hitting some very specific spend path, I feel like the upside gets less exciting unless you’re really using the transfer side a ton.

So yeah, appreciated. I get the appeal, I just think the “cool setup” part can outrun the everyday usefulness pretty easily.

replies.author: u/member_10
replies.content: Appreciate the rent-fee detail — I’m not sure Atmos is worth keeping if it wipes out the rewards.

replies.author: u/member_11
replies.content: Good to know — is everything locked in here, or do you actually have a non-ecosystem option?

replies.author: u/member_12
replies.content: That helps — is it just for Bilt charges, or for everything?

post.title: Are you an AMEX Gold card holder? - Is it worth it and what is your opinion about this offer? - No Travel plans yet...
post.body:
American Express® Gold Card

Earn 100,000 Membership Rewards® points after you spend $6,000 in eligible purchases on your new Card within the first 6 months of Card Membership.†

Annual Fee: $325†¤
Additional Cards (up to the first 5): $0 annual fee
Sixth or more Additional Cards: $35 annual fee per Card.†

comments.author: u/member_01
comments.content: I always thought it was a stupid card until I got it on an upgrade. I love it. Probably comes out of my wallet more than any other card. The credits are easy to use too.

comments.author: u/member_02
comments.content:
Personally I've found the Charles Schwab Platinum and BBP to be the best Amex combo for my situation. You get all the benefits and then some of the personal Gold, plus a premium travel card and a general spend card. Being able to transfer points as cashback to Charles Schwab at a 1.1 c/p is a pretty sweet benefit. 

I can easily recreate the Gold's bonus categories in the aggregate using the Chase Freedom Flex, Discover IT, AAA Daily Advantage, and US Bank Altitude Go, all with no fee.

comments.author: u/member_03
comments.content: It was fun for a couple years but I'm going to dump it. The coupons and the MR points are tiresome to me now.

comments.author: u/member_04
comments.content: I feel like unless you’re high income or live in a large metropolitan area, Cap 1 Savor or Amex BCE or BCP are better options for us normal folk. Simply cannot justify the annual fee myself bc I know I won’t use the credits, but maybe one day

comments.author: u/member_05
comments.content: Unless you have enough spend to easily hit the SUB, most folks are better served by the blue cash preferred.

comments.author: u/member_06
comments.content: It’s definitely a great card and it’s been worth it since 6 years even with AF increase. If you know how to use it the points are amazing. Although I just discovered amazing redemptions about points last year but without that as well it’s been worth it.

comments.author: u/member_07
comments.content: I signed up for the gold card a year ago with that same deal.  I spent $6k and they wouldn't give me the 100,000 points. They found a way to not do what they said. so be warned. I didn't see anything on the online sign-up form that would disqualify me, and they still didn't give it to me

comments.author: u/member_08
comments.content: Only for the first year, and year 2 onwards only if you can get most of the value out of their couponing. If you only get less than 3 quarters of the full value, absolutely not. Not ever. Dont even entertain the idea. A lot of people who say its worth it do not ever consider the opportunity cost. There are lots of catch all 2% back that have no AF. If you consider the points are roughly equivalent to 1 percent cashback and assuming you get an average of 3 points per dollar across all your purchases, you would need to spend 32.5k on the card annually to be more valuable than a 2% catch all. If you have that much money you'd probably have enough money (100k) to be platinum tier in BoA and get their free 2.62% cashback card, where it would take over 80k annual spend on amex to be better than the boa cashback card.

comments.author: u/member_09
comments.content: All Amex cards are worth year 1 because of the the SUB. You come out positive despite fees. year 2 you can make your own assessment if is worth it.

comments.author: u/member_10
comments.content:
IMO the gold was not worth it, It sounds like it on paper getting so many X points. However I was used to cards that 1point = $0.01. Upon looking at redemption options they were all garbage... unless I wanted to play the transfer game, which I did, and got .01 or slightly better, but then I was locked into using them for delta flights, or a specific hotel and I have to book through the Amex travel portal.. which may not be as bad as some.. but is still a travel portal. When comparing prices the portal was charging more than just booking direct, so even if I'm getting better than $0.01 per point, the increase charge generally negated that.

Basically lots of hoops and work to redeem points for anything worth while, and may seem like a deal.. ends up being mediocre. 

I want to simplify my life, so I cancelled, and now use Wells Fargo Active Cash and Autograph. Give me 3x on travel which IS 3% back that I can simply use as a statement credit to pay towards vacations or whatever I want at any time.

This setup is ideal for me because I know I'm getting good returns and I don't have to think about it at all.

comments.author: u/member_11
comments.content:
Used to be until they bumped up the AF$; couldn't (didn't want to) justify spend vs AF so I canceled it.

pre-bump AF was elite top tier for the average city person

comments.author: u/member_12
comments.content: Wait for the 150k offer which comes once or twice a year usually would be what I’d do if considering.

comments.author: u/member_01
comments.content: On its own, 100k MR for $6,000 spend looks pretty solid, even after the $325 AF. If you cash it out at about 1 cpp, that’s roughly $1,000 in value, which still leaves you about $675 ahead before anything else is included. After year one, though, it becomes a keep-or-drop question — without regular use of the 4x categories or credits, the AF starts to matter more.

comments.author: u/member_02
comments.content: Good to know — credits are easy to use

comments.author: u/member_03
comments.content:
100k MR at a 1 cpp floor is already $1,000, so the $325 AF is basically getting covered on paper right there.

that’s the boring math though. the part that made it feel better for me was domestic redemptions — I’ve consistently gotten more than floor on a few US flights, and that’s where the card stopped feeling like “just a SUB machine” and started feeling usable.

I had the same hesitation with the annual fee because it’s not small, but if you’re actually going to redeem MR instead of let them sit, the gap between floor value and real-world value gets pretty wide fast. even a mediocre 1.3 cpp-ish use on 100k is $1,300, which leaves a lot more room after the fee.

I’m not saying it’s magically free money or anything, just that on a straight SUB / fee comparison, the offer clears pretty comfortably for me. if you only ever cash out at the lowest domestic rate, then yeah, the appeal gets thinner, but the bonus itself isn’t the weak part here.

comments.author: u/member_04
comments.content: my “day-to-day spend concentration” is just the card getting sacrificed to the DoorDash gods lol 🙃

comments.author: u/member_05
comments.content: I tried the points route once and, honestly, the hassle of squeezing value out of them killed it for me. The SUB looked nice on paper, but after a few months I was basically doing homework just to beat simple cash back by a little. ended up dropping it and going back to boring cash back... way less annoying.

comments.author: u/member_06
comments.content: For heavy restaurant and grocery spend, those 4X categories are the easy win; once you’re putting enough through it to cover the $325 annual fee, the credits mostly turn into background noise.

comments.author: u/member_07
comments.content: I kept my Gold for ~6 years and it was weirdly fine the whole time, even w/ the AF hanging there. only later did I realize the points / transfer partners side was doing more than I thought, so the “meh” math got better after I changed how I redeemed. still not magic, just ended up being less annoying than I expected.

comments.author: u/member_08
comments.content: I’d say the annoying bit is the 100k SUB not showing up after you’ve already hit the spend. The flow looked clean on my end, which is what makes it worse, since there’s nothing obvious to point at. After that, it turns into the whole support process over something that should’ve been automatic at $6k.

comments.author: u/member_09
comments.content: Yeah, that’s the annoying part — the card only really pencils out in year 1 or if you’re actually chewing through the coupon side hard enough that AF gets buried. Otherwise it’s just negative carry dressed up as “value.” The math on 3 points or whatever is meaningless if the credits sit there unused and your statement balance keeps getting pushed around just to justify the card (which is exactly how they get you). If the utilization is low, the coupon stack is just fake savings, not savings. Same with the $325 type setup: if the spend pattern doesn’t naturally soak it up, the opportunity cost is the real bill. And once you’re past the first-year / product-change gimmick, the whole thing turns into a chore fast. Hard pass unless the coupon utilization is already basically guaranteed.

post.title: Best mix of Credit Cards for Groceries, Gas and Cash Back Catch All?
post.body:
Hey all, So I'm in the process of re-organizing my finances, which includes evaluating my credit cards. I currently have 4:

USAA Platinum Visa: Credit limit - $1,500; Age - 14 years (my first credit card from high school)

Chase Freedom Unlimited: Credit limit - $6,200; Age - 5 yrs, 10 mos

Chase Prime Visa: Credit Limit - $4,700; Age - 4 years, 10 mos

Wells Fargo Active Cash: Credit Limit - $7,500; Age - 11 mos

I want the cards that I have to be good ones for gas, food and cash back, but my goal is to not have more cards to manage which is why I'm debating on closing a card or two.

Here are my thoughts, but I want to get some input from others:

Close my USAA card because honestly it's crap and I don't use it at all. Also close my Freedom Unlimited one. In turn, open the AAA Daily Advantage CC. That would leave me with the AAA for food and gas then the Wells Fargo for my catch all, 2% back on everything else.

My concern is closing 2 cards will hurt my credit score pretty good as the utilization will obviously go up. I don't ever carry a balance and always pay my cards off. I also understand that closing cards doesn't hurt the age as they continue to age, however does closing my 2 oldest affect anything if I'm only looking at opening one?

Ideally, I'd like my mix of cards to all be Chase so I only have one app to manage and see everything, but I don't think that's going to be possible. Hopefully all of this makes sense, just want to make sure I'm thinking everything through before just going for it. If it's recommended I keep them all open, so be it. I'm open to any and all suggestions.

If there are any other questions I need to answer I'm happy to do so. Thank you!

Update: After reading the comments and doing some more research, this is what I'm looking at doing:
1. Getting the AAA Daily Advantage for groceries and Costco Food (Food Card)
2. Getting the Costco Anywhere Visa for Gas (Gas Card)
3. Getting the Citi Double Cash for everything else (Catch All)
4. Keep my Chase Amazon Prime Visa for Amazon
4. Closing my Chase Freedom Unlimited, Wells Fargo Active Cash and USAA Cards - I just don't want to manage all of them/worry about them all.

I'm not going to do this all at once, as I know that would tank my credit, but over a bit of time I'll work on doing that. And I'll apply for the cards first before closing my others.

Thoughts on this?

comments.author: u/member_01
comments.content:
Your plan is solid. AAA Daily Advantage is a great card, and the Active Cash pairs with it well as a catch-all. Many people would also want a Dining card, in which case I would suggest to keep the Freedom Unlimited for that purpose, but if that isn't you, no worries.

Closing your cards will have less of an impact than you believe. Yes, less available credit will translate to a higher utilization, but you'll also be gaining available credit by opening a new card. 

Furthermore, utilization has no memory as a credit metric; as soon as a statement posts with a lower balance, it will replace whatever your previous utilization score was. So you can manipulate your utilization metric as needed if you ever actually need your credit score to be high (which is basically only if you are about to apply for a loan/mortgage).

comments.author: u/member_02
comments.content:
I've been a Citi customer for over 30 years. Citi has saved me from fraud on multiple occasions and the process was always quick and easy. For technical issues you might need to call multiple times until you get a rep who is more knowledgeable, but eventually it always worked out for me. I would rate Wells Fargo's customer service better, but Citi has been on par with Chase and better than Capital One. Amex screwed me on a dispute so I don't particularly like them even though other people do. In short, I think Citi is a good credit card issuer and I wouldn't hesitate to get more of their cards.

As for Citi vs Wells Fargo, if you want a more cash back focused strategy with no annual fee, Wells Fargo is better. They don't have a multiplier for groceries but adding PayPal debit or Citi Custom Cash or both solves that for no annual fee. You can use discount portals like Priceline and Hotwire and save money that way. You still have transfer partners in case you find a good deal. This is a very underrated strategy especially now when points have taken big devaluations. It's not talked about much by influencers because Wells Fargo doesn't pay through referral links like Chase and Amex, but it's probably the best way to go if you're a frugal traveler and want to stretch your dollar.

If you don't mind paying a $95 annual fee and like to play the points and miles game then Citi is better. You can easily justify the $95 annual fee by simply getting good redemptions, and it's easy to do with Citi's transfer partners. The welcome bonus for Strata Premier is big enough to justify trying it out and figuring out if it's for you. You can downgrade to Custom Cash if you'd rather go with a cash back setup.

comments.author: u/member_03
comments.content:
Between the two, I would go CIti for two main reasons. First, Citi has much better transfer partners and second, WF currently doesn't have a card with multipliers on groceries which is a huge category to leave uncovered.

I personally would target a hybrid approach and pick up specific cards from both issuers as a starting point. Especially consider targeting the Strata Premier and the Active Cash early, and then lay out a road map to eventually pick up the Strata, Double Cash, Custom Cahse, Attune and Autograph. After you have the first two cards, just pick these up in the order that makes sense for you and that best follows the rules of the two banks. When you are finished you have a really strong setup with only a $95 annual fee to contend with.

If you do happen to have a use case for the $100 credit, then that'll just be the cherry on top. This of course assumes that partners such as AA, Choice, IPrefer are of value to you.

You mentioned you have plans to get a custom cash at some point. If you go with Citi, you might also be interested in getting **multiple** custom cash cards to optimize 5% in various categories.

post.title: Any recommendations to simplify/reduce my number of cards or maximize cash back or points?
post.body: My wife and I recently got the US Bank Smartly card (v.1, the not yet nerfed one) with 4% back. I’ve collected some cards over the years, collecting sign up bonuses, capitalizing on 0% APR, and otherwise. I focus on cash back instead of miles. My thought with that is that it’s easier to just convert the points to cash on a regular basis and then put the cash into savings or payments or whatever. I’m somewhat interested in the opportunity to get more bang for the buck via travel rewards (like via Chase Sapphire), but I’m not sure I’m there yet or convinced yet. Current strategy is to use the Amazon Prime Visa for the fair amount of shopping we do at Whole Foods and Amazon, use the Discover and Freedom rotating categories, and then use the US Bank Smartly for everything else (including tax payments that I’m planning to start with next quarter). Given that strategy, my thought is to close the cards I don’t need for that strategy or that aren’t particular helpful, even if they are older cards that closing may bring down my average card age. Of the cards below, I’m thinking about closing the Chase Unlimited Freedom, Chase Sapphire, and Citi AAdvantage cards now and closing the BofA Americard and Wells Fargo Reflect card after the 0% APR expires and we pay off the balances. We don’t travel abroad a whole lot (maybe once every couple years), but we possibly have some extended travel (3+ months) coming up in the next year. The Amazon Prime has no foreign transaction fees, but I am thinking to keep the Capital One Quicksilver as another no foreign transaction fee card option, and one with a higher credit limit. I’m also cognizant of the possibly that my US Bank Smartly card could get nerfed in the near future. Build a spreadsheet, dump your annual spend on it, calculate the *marginal* value of each card and whether they're worth keeping/getting.  Close cards you don't use/value.

post.title: Can I switch the type of BoA card I have if I just got one?
post.body:
So I recently got the Bank of America Travel Rewards for Students. I thought I was going to get 3 points per transaction that was considered travel, but it's actually 3 points for travel made through their travel center. Despite it being written on the terms and agreements when I signed up, it just didn't click and I didn't understand what that meant until now that I've already gotten the card and used it. I only really wanted the card to maximize savings and use it to buy Amtrak tickets, but you can't even buy Amtrak tickets through their travel center. You can redeem your points for an Amtrak gift card, but the cashback equivalent for gift cards comes out to 0.8%, and I already have the Discover It student card so I feel like atp buying tickets with my discover card would be better. 

 
So I went back to the BoA student credit cards and I think the Customized Cash Rewards card might be better? This one gives you 3% cash back for a category of your choice, which I would make travel. And from my understanding rn, I don't need to do it through a travel center. My question is, if I did want to make this switch can I just call the bank and get it swapped out if I've already used the old one, paid the balance, and got the sign up reward point bonus for it? Or is there any benefit to keeping this card? 

 
Thanks, I just want a little help and info before I call and sound even more dumb lol.

comments.author: u/member_01
comments.content:
Use the Travel Rewards card as an everyday catch-all card to earn the signup bonus, and then to earn $.015 everywhere, then just redeem for statement credits against your Amtrak purchases.

if you're going to be spending lots on Amtrak or other travel, the Customized Cash could make more sense. Some other things to consider:

- If you set your 3% category to online purchases, many travel purchases should qualify. I don't know specifically about Amtrak, but even if it isn't included, you can change the category once a month. So you could toggle between travel and online shopping once a month between travel and online shopping depending on your spending patterns.)

- Bank of America has historically combined credit inquiries for applications within 30 days or less. I don't know if this is still the case, but it was for me about a year ago. If you think you would be better off with a different BoA card, it is likely that you won't get another hard credit inquiry.

- It's worth looking at the Premium Rewards card, maybe down the road. It earns an unlimited 2 points per dollar on travel and dining, and 1.5 points per dollar on everything else (redeemable at one cent per point as cashback or travel credits.) It has a $95 annual fee, but provides a $100 travel credit for airline incidental fees. (I have used this for American Airlines gift cards, YMMV with other airlines.)

- If you start saving/investing with Bank of America/Merrill, they reward your relationship by giving bonuses on credit card rewards. As a student, it's worth considering opening a retirement account like a Roth account at Merrill. At the highest tier, you can get a 75% bonus on credit card earnings, meaning that you would earn 5.25% on the selected Customized Cash card (up to $2,500 spent per quarter), unlimited 3.5 points/cents per dollar on travel/ dining with the Premium Rewards card, and 2.62 cents back on the Travel Rewards/Premium Rewards cards.

- I don't think they have student versions, but FNBO issues Amtrak credit cards. The one with the $99 annual fee sometimes offers a 40,000 point signup bonus and earns 3 points per dollar on Amtrak purchases, while the no annual fee version earns 2 points per dollar on Amtrak purchases. Amtrak points can be pretty valuable, and you also get a 5% rebate on redemptions wirh both cards, so it could be worth getting one of them in the future.

Good luck!

comments.author: u/member_02
comments.content: Typically issuers won't do product changes until you've had the card for a year (maybe 6 months). I'm not sure what BofA's policy is on product changes in this case. There's no harm in calling and asking.

replies.author: u/member_03
replies.content: Yeah, I called right now, and they told me I can't do a product change. I'd have to put in a new application. Will it hurt my credit score that bad if I apply for it already?

comments.content:
1. You can buy an Amtrak ticket on the card and then redeem the points to cover the ticket on the Rewards website at 1¢/point.

2. You must call and ask about product changes on the telephone. Whether they will tends to vary by employee. Call at least twice before giving up. 

This card doesn't have an annual fee, so maybe it's possible to product change it when it's less than a year old. If you call twice now and they both say no it could be worth trying again once the account is over a year old to see if you can get a product change then.

replies.author: u/member_03
replies.content:
1. For the amtrak gift card: I was thinking of doing that maybe with the points I have right now, but their website says 3,125 points = $25. Isn't that like saying I get 0.8% cash back so it wouldn't be worth it? When I called, they said I could redeem my points for a travel statement credit instead where 2,500 points is $25 which is the same thing as like 1% cash back right. So maybe that's better if I ever want those 3 points, I need to make purchases through the travel center, but I don't think I'd use it that much. 

2. And idk cuz when I called and asked to replace it, they just said that card isn't eligible to change but the other ones are. 🤷‍♀️

Could I also just apply for the third card right now? Is there any harm/benefit to doing that?

comments.author: u/member_01
comments.content:
I’d keep the current card for everyday spend a bit longer, honestly... if you’re still in the window where the points are worth finishing out, that’s the cleanest way to squeeze the last bit of value before messing with anything.

Then just burn the value on the travel side when it makes sense. If the redemption path is basically statement credit against Amtrak, that’s usually the part that matters more than the card itself... the earn rate on random spend can look fine on paper, but if the redemption is weak or capped weirdly, the math gets ugly fast.

I’ve seen people treat a card like a catch-all just because it’s already in the wallet, and that works only if the points actually clear a decent floor. If the alternative student card is giving you better straight cash-back on normal purchases, that may fit the use case better than forcing everything through the Amtrak setup.

Also, the annual fee piece matters more than people want to admit. A $95 annual fee or a $99 annual fee card can be fine if you’re using the travel redemption often enough, but if you’re not, it starts acting like dead weight pretty quickly. Same deal if you’re only trying to protect a small amount of value... 30 days here, 2

My thought with that is that it’s easier to just convert the points to cash on a regular basis and then put the cash into savings or payments or whatever. I’m somewhat interested in the opportunity to get more bang for the buck via travel rewards (like via Chase Sapphire), but I’m not sure I’m there yet or convinced yet. Current strategy is to use the Amazon Prime Visa for the fair amount of shopping we do at Whole Foods and Amazon, use the Discover and Freedom rotating categories, and then use the US Bank Smartly for everything else (including tax payments that I’m planning to start with next quarter). We don’t travel abroad a whole lot (maybe once every couple years), but we possibly have some extended travel (3+ months) coming up in the next year. comments.content:
I’m going to be the annoying optimization guy here: your setup is already close to efficient, but I think you’re focusing a little too hard on trimming the card count versus maximizing usable return.

A few blunt points:
- **Keep the Capital One Quicksilver** as your clean, no-drama catch-all if you want simplicity. It’s not flashy, but a consistent 1.5%+ baseline on uncategorized spend is better than holding dead weight.
- **Don’t cancel Chase Sapphire just because you’re “mostly cashback.”** If you ever want transfer flexibility or travel protections, keeping the option open is often smarter than torching it.
- **The real priority is the promo debt.** The $20.5k in 0% balances matters way more than whether you have 6 cards or 9 cards.
- **US Bank Smartly at 4% is fantastic if it survives, but don’t build your whole strategy around issuer goodwill.** Banks nerf products all the time.

If I were simplifying this, I’d keep:
1. Smartly for catch-all while it lasts
2. Amazon Prime for Amazon/Whole Foods
3. Quicksilver for no-FX / backup spending
4. One travel-flex card only if you genuinely use the benefits

Everything else is mostly overlap. The best cashback strategy is the one you can actually run consistently without overthinking every transaction.

post.body:
I just got my Social Security, a friend of mine suggested [Discover chrome for students](https://www.discover.com/credit-cards/student-credit-card/chrome-card.html?ICMPGN=ALL_CC_STUDENT_CHROME_CARD), a family member suggested [Discover Cashback Credit](https://www.discover.com/credit-cards/cash-back/it-card.html?ICMPGN=ALL_CC_CB_CARD). 
I'm a student, I don't have a steady source of income, but I'm on a stipend from my parents, not sure on which of these 2 cards would be better for me.

The Cashback Credit it seems like the 5% cashback offer, but it changes every quarter, that might be a bit difficult to keep track, Chrome for student has 2% cashback on Gas stations and restaurants, I don't have a car(no gas money), I try not to eat out frequently(unless chinese restaurants at the corner count as a restaurant).

I would have just gone with the Chrome for students, but I think the family member might be onto something for the Cashback credit. 

Requirements:

Ease of building credit, I can sacrifice cashback if one is a lot easier to build my credit score with.

Edit: this is my first card.

comments.author: u/member_01
comments.content:
There is no credit card that "builds credit" (including your score) any better than the next.  All credit cards accomplish this in the same way.

The question I have is whether you're talking secured cards or unsecured cards.  Your post is suggestive of this being your first card, but you don't specifically state that so it would be important to know.  Also do you have ANY accounts at all on your credit report... open or closed... cards or loans?  Without any credit at all, going with a secured card is the smarter "sure bet" to avoid a denial.  If you have some credit history already, going with an unsecured card may be an option for you.

replies.author: u/member_02
replies.content:
First credit card, no credit history.
What’s secured and unsecured card?

replies.author: u/member_01
replies.content: A secured card is a line of credit that you "secure" with a deposit.  This could be something like $200-$500.  That deposit becomes your credit limit.  This eliminates the risk that lender would normally assume when you get an unsecured card (no deposit).  A secured card is much easier to get approved for on a zero history file since lenders often don't want to hand over unsecured credit (and take on risk) with someone that hasn't proven anything credit history wise yet.  With a secured card you typically can ask after roughly 12 months to "graduate" it to an unsecured version and get back whatever the initial deposit was that you put down to get the card.

replies.author: u/member_02
replies.content: I think would be going with an unsecured card.

replies.author: u/member_01
replies.content: You are welcome to try, just know that there are mixed results when going for an unsecured card out of the gate.  It could result in a denial, where if you stick with a secured card it will be an easy approval.

post.title: Can I switch the type of BoA card I have if I just got one?
post.body:
So I recently got the Bank of America Travel Rewards for Students. I thought I was going to get 3 points per transaction that was considered travel, but it's actually 3 points for travel made through their travel center. Despite it being written on the terms and agreements when I signed up, it just didn't click and I didn't understand what that meant until now that I've already gotten the card and used it. I only really wanted the card to maximize savings and use it to buy Amtrak tickets, but you can't even buy Amtrak tickets through their travel center. You can redeem your points for an Amtrak gift card, but the cashback equivalent for gift cards comes out to 0.8%, and I already have the Discover It student card so I feel like atp buying tickets with my discover card would be better. 

 
So I went back to the BoA student credit cards and I think the Customized Cash Rewards card might be better? This one gives you 3% cash back for a category of your choice, which I would make travel. And from my understanding rn, I don't need to do it through a travel center. My question is, if I did want to make this switch can I just call the bank and get it swapped out if I've already used the old one, paid the balance, and got the sign up reward point bonus for it? Or is there any benefit to keeping this card? 

 
Thanks, I just want a little help and info before I call and sound even more dumb lol.

comments.author: u/member_01
comments.content:
Use the Travel Rewards card as an everyday catch-all card to earn the signup bonus, and then to earn $.015 everywhere, then just redeem for statement credits against your Amtrak purchases.

if you're going to be spending lots on Amtrak or other travel, the Customized Cash could make more sense. Some other things to consider:

- If you set your 3% category to online purchases, many travel purchases should qualify. I don't know specifically about Amtrak, but even if it isn't included, you can change the category once a month. So you could toggle between travel and online shopping once a month between travel and online shopping depending on your spending patterns.)

- Bank of America has historically combined credit inquiries for applications within 30 days or less. I don't know if this is still the case, but it was for me about a year ago. If you think you would be better off with a different BoA card, it is likely that you won't get another hard credit inquiry.

- It's worth looking at the Premium Rewards card, maybe down the road. It earns an unlimited 2 points per dollar on travel and dining, and 1.5 points per dollar on everything else (redeemable at one cent per point as cashback or travel credits.) It has a $95 annual fee, but provides a $100 travel credit for airline incidental fees. (I have used this for American Airlines gift cards, YMMV with other airlines.)

- If you start saving/investing with Bank of America/Merrill, they reward your relationship by giving bonuses on credit card rewards. As a student, it's worth considering opening a retirement account like a Roth account at Merrill. At the highest tier, you can get a 75% bonus on credit card earnings, meaning that you would earn 5.25% on the selected Customized Cash card (up to $2,500 spent per quarter), unlimited 3.5 points/cents per dollar on travel/ dining with the Premium Rewards card, and 2.62 cents back on the Travel Rewards/Premium Rewards cards.

- I don't think they have student versions, but FNBO issues Amtrak credit cards. The one with the $99 annual fee sometimes offers a 40,000 point signup bonus and earns 3 points per dollar on Amtrak purchases, while the no annual fee version earns 2 points per dollar on Amtrak purchases. Amtrak points can be pretty valuable, and you also get a 5% rebate on redemptions wirh both cards, so it could be worth getting one of them in the future.

Good luck!

comments.content: Typically issuers won't do product changes until you've had the card for a year (maybe 6 months). I'm not sure what BofA's policy is on product changes in this case. There's no harm in calling and asking.

replies.author: u/member_03
replies.content: Yeah, I called right now, and they told me I can't do a product change. I'd have to put in a new application. Will it hurt my credit score that bad if I apply for it already?

So maybe that's better if I ever want those 3 points, I need to make purchases through the travel center, but I don't think I'd use it that much. 

2. And idk cuz when I called and asked to replace it, they just said that card isn't eligible to change but the other ones are. 🤷‍♀️

comments.author: u/member_01
comments.content: Yep, you can usually do a product change, but it’s best to call BoA and ask what options are available for your account. The big thing is whether you’ve already earned the signup bonus—some reps are okay with a switch after that, but you want to confirm before changing anything. Also, if your goal is Amtrak, I’d compare the true redemption value carefully because “travel” categories can get oddly restrictive fast. BoA can be a solid keeper if you can use the category well, but if not, the better move is usually the card that gives you straightforward redemption without extra hoops.

comments.author: u/member_02
comments.content:
Ugh, I feel this so much 😅 I’d probably call BoA and ask about a product change too. The Travel Rewards sounds super misleading if it only works through their travel center, especially if your actual goal is Amtrak tickets. The Customized Cash Rewards seems way more flexible if you can set travel as your category.

Also, definitely not a dumb question — credit card terms are weirdly easy to misunderstand at first.

comments.author: u/member_03
comments.content: Totally agree that a product change is worth asking about here. If your goal is Amtrak and flexible travel redemptions, the Travel Rewards for Students sounds pretty restrictive compared with Customized Cash Rewards. I’d call BoA after your SUB posts and ask specifically whether they can switch you without losing any earned benefits or account history. Also, since you’re already using Discover for general spend, I’d focus on keeping the card that gives you the cleanest cash back or travel value with the fewest hoops.

comments.author: u/member_04
comments.content:
Worth sanity-checking the EV before you product-change. If you’re targeting Amtrak, the “3x travel” on Travel Rewards for Students is usually a poor fit if the travel portal doesn’t include your actual spend path.

Roughly speaking, a flat 3% category card on real travel is far more usable than a portal-restricted 3x structure, because the effective return only matters on spend you can actually route through the portal. If BoA lets you PC into Customized Cash Rewards and set travel as the 3% category, that’s the cleaner setup for direct Amtrak purchases.

I’d call and ask 3 things:
1) Can this account be product-changed?
2) Will the existing SUB stay intact?
3) Can the new product keep the same open date / history?

If the answer to #1 and #2 is yes, I’d probably switch. If not, it may be worth keeping the current card as a no-fee placeholder only if it helps your overall BoA relationship/credit age.

comments.author: u/member_05
comments.content:
Honestly, if Amtrak is the main goal, I’d push you toward the Customized Cash Rewards over the Travel Rewards for Students too 🙂 The travel-center restriction makes the original card way less flexible than it sounds, which is super frustrating after the fact.

If you’ve already gotten the SUB and are okay with a product change, calling BoA is the right move. Just ask specifically whether you can switch to CCR without messing up your bonus or account history. If they allow it, that sounds like the cleaner fit for you. And you’re not dumb at all — BoA naming/terms can be sneaky confusing 😅

comments.author: u/member_06
comments.content: This is such a relatable mistake honestly — credit card terms can be weirdly sneaky at first. If your main goal is Amtrak, I’d definitely ask BoA about a product change to Customized Cash Rewards and make sure you specifically ask whether the SUB and account age stay intact. That flexibility would probably help more than the portal-only setup on the Travel Rewards for Students.

comments.author: u/member_03
comments.content: I’m pretty frugal, so I’d only consider Wells Fargo if the rewards were simple and the value was easy to keep without paying an annual fee. The Autograph does look decent on paper, but I’d compare it against a straightforward 2% cashback card first since that’s usually easier to maximize without extra hassle. For me, the bank reputation matters too, but the biggest thing is whether the card actually saves money in real life.

comments.author: u/member_04
comments.content:
The short version: people dislike Wells Fargo because the reputation issues aren’t just vibes — they’ve had repeated trust/oversight problems, and that matters a lot when you’re choosing a financial institution.

On the Autograph specifically, I’d separate the bank from the card:
- If you only care about card value, compare the earn rates and redemption value against 2% cash back / no-AF alternatives
- If you care about ecosystem, service, and reliability, Wells Fargo’s baggage should absolutely be part of the decision

So no, you’re not missing some hidden magic. The card can be decent, but “decent on paper” isn’t enough if the simpler options are easier to maximize and easier to trust.

comments.author: u/member_05
comments.content:
I think you’re seeing two different things get mixed together: bank reputation and card value. Wells Fargo’s baggage definitely makes people wary, but the Autograph itself can still be decent if you actually use the categories and don’t mind the ecosystem.

That said, from a points-for-value perspective I still lean simple: if a card is harder to optimize than a no-AF cashback option, it’s usually not worth the hassle unless the earn rates clearly beat the alternatives you already use.

post.title: Discover Cashback Credit vs Discover Chrome for students
post.body:
I just got my Social Security, a friend of mine suggested [Discover chrome for students](https://www.discover.com/credit-cards/student-credit-card/chrome-card.html?ICMPGN=ALL_CC_STUDENT_CHROME_CARD), a family member suggested [Discover Cashback Credit](https://www.discover.com/credit-cards/cash-back/it-card.html?ICMPGN=ALL_CC_CB_CARD). 
I'm a student, I don't have a steady source of income, but I'm on a stipend from my parents, not sure on which of these 2 cards would be better for me.

The Cashback Credit it seems like the 5% cashback offer, but it changes every quarter, that might be a bit difficult to keep track, Chrome for student has 2% cashback on Gas stations and restaurants, I don't have a car(no gas money), I try not to eat out frequently(unless chinese restaurants at the corner count as a restaurant).

I would have just gone with the Chrome for students, but I think the family member might be onto something for the Cashback credit. 

Requirements:

Ease of building credit, I can sacrifice cashback if one is a lot easier to build my credit score with.

Edit: this is my first card.

comments.author: u/member_01
comments.content:
There is no credit card that "builds credit" (including your score) any better than the next.  All credit cards accomplish this in the same way.

The question I have is whether you're talking secured cards or unsecured cards.  Your post is suggestive of this being your first card, but you don't specifically state that so it would be important to know.  Also do you have ANY accounts at all on your credit report... open or closed... cards or loans?  Without any credit at all, going with a secured card is the smarter "sure bet" to avoid a denial.  If you have some credit history already, going with an unsecured card may be an option for you.

replies.author: u/member_02
replies.content:
First credit card, no credit history.
What’s secured and unsecured card?

replies.author: u/member_01
replies.content: A secured card is a line of credit that you "secure" with a deposit.  This could be something like $200-$500.  That deposit becomes your credit limit.  This eliminates the risk that lender would normally assume when you get an unsecured card (no deposit).  A secured card is much easier to get approved for on a zero history file since lenders often don't want to hand over unsecured credit (and take on risk) with someone that hasn't proven anything credit history wise yet.  With a secured card you typically can ask after roughly 12 months to "graduate" it to an unsecured version and get back whatever the initial deposit was that you put down to get the card.

replies.author: u/member_02
replies.content: I think would be going with an unsecured card.

replies.content: You are welcome to try, just know that there are mixed results when going for an unsecured card out of the gate.  It could result in a denial, where if you stick with a secured card it will be an easy approval.
